items.title: AI - Mars. Autonomous Multi-Material Self-Replicating Factory (AM-SRF) & Advanced Nuclear Micro-Battery Production for Deep-Space AI Infrastructure
items.abstract: Autonomous Multi-Material Self-Replicating Factory (AM-SRF) & Advanced Nuclear Micro-Battery Production for Deep-Space AI Infrastructure Abstract & System Overview The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence into deep space—specifically targeting the hostile, high-radiation environments of the Moon and Mars—demands an unprecedented paradigm shift in power generation, manufacturing autonomy, and resilience. Traditional silicon-based electronics and solar arrays fail under severe cosmic radiation, thermal fluctuations, and dust storms. To solve this, we introduce the Autonomous Multi-Material Self-Replicating Factory (AM-SRF), a unified single-module manufacturing system integrated with advanced isotope gas handling circuits, laser-assisted Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD), and poly-diamond nuclear micro-batteries. Powered by isotope-derived energy and resilient against planetary radiation, this infrastructure enables AI systems to construct their own habitats, manufacture industrial machinery, execute self-repair protocols, and harvest extraterrestrial resources such as helium-3. 1. Unified Single-Module Manufacturing Architecture (The "1-Machine" Concept) Unlike terrestrial multi-factory supply chains that rely on fragile logistics, the AM-SRF consolidates the entire production chain into a single, highly optimized growth and post-processing module. Isotope Gas Handling & Recirculation: The system features a closed-loop isotope recovery circuit connected to high-purity precursor gas tanks (such as \bm{98\%} enriched \bm{^{14}\text{CH}_4} or tritium-doped precursors). Mass flow controllers regulate gas delivery into a coaxial injection nozzle, while a recirculation pump and mixing valve capture unreacted gases, scrub impurities with clean \bm{\text{H}_2} carrier gas, and maintain optimal reaction pressures. Dynamic CVD Chamber: At the core of the machine is a hermetically sealed quartz and sapphire reaction chamber. A UV laser beam path, focused via high-precision lenses onto a rotating molybdenum disc substrate, drives layer-by-layer crystalline growth. In-Process Feedback & Laser Slicing: Automated optical probes and re-counter feedback mechanisms monitor layer uniformity and thickness in real time. Integrated laser cutting modules slice the grown crystalline boules into precise planar and spherical micro-battery arrays and structural components without breaking vacuum. 2. Advanced Material Science: Poly-Diamonds, Tritium, and Carbon-14 The operational longevity and radiation immunity of deep-space AI systems depend entirely on the material composition of their power sources and structural chassis. The AM-SRF produces batteries utilizing the following stacked material specifications: Transitional Layers (\bm{5\text{--}10\text{ nm}}): Single-crystal Carbon-14 (\bm{\text{sp}^3+\text{sp}^2} hybridization) providing exceptional p-type or n-type conductivity and atomic bonding integrity between the substrate and active cathode. Carbon-14 & Tritium Doped Diamond Cathodes (\bm{1\text{--}2\ \mu\text{m}}): Utilizing beta-voltaic conversion within a diamond lattice matrix. Diamond's wide bandgap (\bm{\sim5.5\text{ eV}}) and high displacement threshold energy make it impervious to radiation damage. Beta particles emitted by \bm{^{14}\text{C}} or tritium generate electron-hole pairs continuously for millennia without external recharging. Polyimide-Diamond Deposition Layers (\bm{10\text{--}20\ \mu\text{m}}): Polymer-matrix composite layers reinforced with carbon isotope doping, delivering superior mechanical strength, fracture toughness, and thermal dissipation. Substrates and Current Collectors: High-purity single-crystal diamond and copper-coated polymer substrates ensure efficient ion transport and ultra-low internal resistance, achieving energy densities exceeding \bm{2.60\text{ kW}\cdot\text{hr}/\text{cm}^3}. 3. Radiation Immunity and Deep-Space Survival Martian and lunar environments present lethal radiation hazards, including Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCRs) and Solar Particle Events (SPEs), which instantly degrade standard semiconductor architectures. Diamond Lattice Hardening: The nuclear micro-batteries and structural chassis produced by the AM-SRF utilize radiation-hardened diamond structures. Because carbon-14 and tritium beta decays are harnessed directly within the wide-bandgap diamond lattice, incoming external ionizing radiation is safely dissipated through collective lattice phonon interactions rather than generating destructive charge trapping. Self-Healing Electronic Substrates: The AI systems powered by these batteries operate within redundant fractal-wave network architectures. If micro-meteorite impacts or localized radiation spikes damage a circuit path, the AM-SRF's robotic manipulators and laser-cutting tools can instantly manufacture and swap replacement modules on the fly. 4. Autonomous City Construction and Self-Replication An AI governed by this infrastructure is not a passive tool, but an active planetary constructor. In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU): Using the AM-SRF's integrated regolith processing modules, the system extracts raw silicates, carbon, and metal oxides from lunar and Martian dust. Automated Scaling and Expansion: The factory uses its linear-rotary carrier tracks and multi-axis robotic arms to fabricate structural bricks, radiation-shielded habitats, solar-thermal mirrors, and additional CVD growth units. By replicating its own machinery, a single initial seed unit can expand into an industrial network capable of building entire subsurface cities and manufacturing plants autonomously. 5. Helium-3 Integration and Deep-Space Expansion As the AI colony expands its industrial footprint across the solar system, reliance on terrestrial-sourced isotopes transitions to abundant extraterrestrial resources. Transition to He-3 Fusion: The AM-SRF architecture is natively engineered to incorporate Helium-3 (\bm{^3\text{He}}) recovery and fusion energy integration. Lunar regolith, enriched with solar-wind-implanted helium-3 over billions of years, is harvested, thermally processed, and fed into advanced compact fusion reactors. Limitless Power for Deep Space: By shifting from beta-voltaic micro-batteries to localized He-3 fusion generators produced by the same self-replicating machinery, the AI obtains the massive energy throughput required for heavy manufacturing, atmospheric terraforming, and interstellar propulsion. items.title: AI Adoption at Higher Education Institutions: A Call for Designated AI Management
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming teaching, learning and administration in higher education institutions (HEIs), yet responsibility for its governance is rarely assigned. This article develops and empirically tests the profile of an AI Manager for HEIs proposed by the Erasmus+ project FORCE AI. A literature-based definition and nine-area competence profile were examined in a sequential mixed-methods study, a survey of 387 students and staff from 13 countries and five nominal-group focus groups in Germany, Latvia, the Netherlands, and Türkiye in 2025, which tested the elements stakeholders can rate: competences, responsibilities, placement, and qualifications. Only 17% of respondents knew of a designated AI-management responsibility at their institution; of the remainder, 71% considered one necessary and 76% expected an AI Manager to improve their experience. The expected mandate comprised training, ethical oversight, data security and strategy; preferences were split between a dedicated position and a shared cross-functional function. Survey respondents portrayed the role as a compliance-oriented technical specialist, whereas staff-dominated focus groups, rating the same competencies, prioritised leadership, change and project management, and communication alongside AI expertise and ethics; this contrast between methods and samples persists for staff respondents alone. The revised definition and profile position designated AI management, a dedicated AI Manager or a team with an accountable lead, as change leadership with technical credibility and give HEIs a tested basis for establishing this role.

items.title: AI and Classroom Assessment in Pre-service Teacher Education: A Bibliometric Analysis of Research Trends, Thematic Evolution, and Future Directions
items.abstract: Assessment preparation in teacher education remains a persistent concern as pre-service teachers are increasingly expected to design valid assessments, generate meaningful feedback, interpret learning evidence, and exercise professional judgment in AI-mediated classrooms. This study presents a bibliometric analysis of research on artificial intelligence-enhanced classroom assessment in pre-service teacher education from 2005 to 2025. Using Scopus-indexed publications, the study analyzed 344 documents from 242 sources to map publication trends, citation patterns, influential authors and institutions, geographic distribution, co-citation structures, keyword co-occurrence networks, and thematic evolution. Results show that the field is young but rapidly expanding, with an annual growth rate of 29.61% and a sharp increase in publications from 2022 onward, reflecting the growing influence of generative AI, ChatGPT, automated feedback, learning analytics, and intelligent learning systems. Co-citation analysis revealed three intellectual foundations: teacher knowledge and research foundations, generative AI-mediated pedagogical practice, formative feedback and automated assessment. Keyword co-occurrence analysis identified four major thematic clusters: AI integration and ethical teacher education, intelligent learning systems and data-driven student learning, AI-supported feedback and personalization, and assessment analytics and evidence-based grading. The findings suggest that AI-enhanced classroom assessment is not merely a technological issue but a pedagogical and professional concern requiring assessment literacy, AI literacy, ethical judgment, and teacher agency. The study contributes a field-level understanding of this emerging research domain and highlights the need for more focused, ethical, and context-sensitive studies on how pre-service teachers design, evaluate, and use AI-supported classroom assessments.

items.title: AI as a Thinking Partner in Sustainability-Oriented Mathematical Modelling: An Exploratory Study of Pre-Service Teachers’ Comparative Reflection
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is mostly used in education to generate solutions, provide feedback or support instruction; approaches that use AI outputs as objects of comparison and reflection remain less explored. This small-scale exploratory qualitative case study examined AI-supported comparative reflection in sustainability-oriented mathematical modelling. Twelve pre-service mathematics teachers individually developed models for a task on water use in a school garden and then compared them with a model produced by ChatGPT (GPT-4o), reflecting on the comparison in writing. Modelling products, written comparisons and reflection forms were analysed using inductive content analysis. The comparison prompted participants to question assumptions, identify limitations in both models and consider alternative variables and representations; most described how they would revise their models. Their accounts contained indications of critical, creative and metacognitive reasoning. However, several participants treated the AI output as an answer key, some of their critiques echoed weaknesses that the AI had listed about itself, and none noticed a computational inconsistency deliberately retained in the output. As the design included no comparison condition or pre–post measure, the findings describe patterns of reasoning displayed during the activity, not improvements in thinking skills or modelling competence. Implications for teacher education are discussed.

items.title: AI as assistant, not creative co-author: AI imaginaries among Social Cartoon Influencers in Vietnam
items.abstract: Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have intensified debates about automation, authorship, and labour across creative industries. Yet these discussions are often dominated by disruption and replacement narratives, leaving limited attention to how creators interpret and negotiate AI in everyday practice, particularly in non-Western contexts. This paper examines how Social Cartoon Influencers (SCIs) in Vietnam interpret and use GenAI within their routine creative production. The study combines semi-structured interviews and contextual observations of production workflows through the lens of AI imaginaries. Findings reveal that creators position AI as a creative assistant rather than a co-author, using it for ideation, optimisation and routine tasks, while reserving final authorship for humans. The clear human-AI boundary results from concerns surrounding situated notions of authenticity and ‘national tone’. The paper argues that AI adoption is shaped by negotiated boundaries around authorship, authenticity, and cultural legitimacy.

items.title: AI Dividend Accounting Framework for the United States: Mathematical Specification, Conditional Applications and Reproducibility Package
items.abstract: Additional production does not translate automatically into household income. This working paper presents a reproducible accounting framework for tracing a stated AI-related production scenario through capital consumption, cross-border income, corporate saving, taxes and transfers to resident income and household groups. Australia was the first implementation. This United States application examines the framework under different institutional arrangements, including substantial income from abroad, retained corporate profits and pension-income attribution. It uses US Bureau of Economic Analysis sources and selected scenario settings from the Yale Budget Lab’s AI-Fiscal project. It does not replicate the Budget Lab’s tax model. The contribution is an explicit, inspectable measurement protocol: definitions and equations specify the required inputs; accounting checks reconcile the flows; and evidence labels distinguish reported observations, derived quantities, assumptions and unidentified results. Missing evidence is not silently replaced with zero. In four selected Moderate cases using a 2025 base, with government retaining additional revenue, household income ranges from USD 25.20 to USD 49.32 per USD 100 of additional production. Net resident income ranges from USD 55.96 to USD 82.62 per USD 100 of additional production. These differences illustrate the consequences of source factor-share assumptions and alternative foreign-income responses. They are selected conditional cases, not confidence intervals or estimates of realised US AI gains. The specification preserves the annual illustration using 2023 household component proxies. A separately dated application uses provisional 2024 group proxies and runs Q2 2026 conditional cases with explicitly carried-forward annual recipient ratios. These applications are not a time series of measured AI effects. The empirical real net dividend per person remains unidentified. Editorial release 0.3.1 preserves the computational core and dated application unchanged while clarifying definitions, fiscal labels, aggregation, rounding and presentation. The deposit includes an expert summary, mathematical specification, latest-data report, executable replication package and verification receipt. ChatGPT assisted development and internal verification; Claude was used for separate AI-assisted audits of earlier work. Independent human scientific validation remains outstanding. Research and release responsibility rests with Muhammad Imran Khan, acting in a personal capacity; no employer or institutional endorsement is implied. Author-owned documents and results are licensed under CC BY 4.0; code is MIT-licensed. Third-party materials retain their own terms. Readers should begin with the one-page expert summary. Feedback is particularly welcome on the scenario-to-national-accounts mapping, institutional boundaries and evidence needed to establish marginal household incidence. items.title: AI Labour Rights Awareness and Career Adaptation Confidence among Respondents in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence changes both the skills used at work and the conditions under which employment decisions are made. Awareness of these changes does not necessarily coincide with confidence in adapting a career. This study examines that distinction in 385 adult, AI-aware survey records from Bangladesh, including 238 law students and 61 respondents classified as law graduates. Five statements separately assess awareness of workplace rights and responsibilities, recognition of protection from unfair automated decisions, reported complementary skill development, adaptation confidence and the perceived preparedness benefit of understanding labour issues. Analyses combine full response distributions, joint endorsement patterns, paired comparisons, ordinal correlations and an exploratory proportional-odds model. Recognition of the need for protection was endorsed by 79.2%, compared with 48.8% endorsing adaptation confidence, a paired difference of 30.4 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval 23.9–36.6). General rights awareness and skill development had small positive ordinal associations with confidence. In the adjusted ordinal model, their odds ratios were 1.30 (95% interval 1.04–1.61; Holm p = 0.038) and 1.40 (1.09–1.79; Holm p = 0.024) respectively. The protection-recognition estimate was less certain, although the two awareness coefficients were not demonstrably different. The findings distinguish rights recognition, reported action and confidence rather than establish a causal awareness-to-adaptability pathway. They support evaluating legal-literacy education alongside practical career tasks and institutional safeguards. The mixed sample, study-specific single items, undocumented recruitment and fieldwork dates, and source-documentation limitations constrain inference. A subsequent study should use verified graduate eligibility, independent legal-knowledge assessments and longitudinal career outcomes.

items.title: AI Literacy and AI Anxiety as Differential Correlates of Positive and Negative Attitudes Towards Artificial Intelligence Among Speech and Language Therapists in Türkiye
items.abstract: Abstract Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied in speech and language therapy (SLT). Evidence on SLTs’ attitudes towards it has been largely descriptive, generated with study-specific questionnaires or with validated attitude scales analysed descriptively. The psychological factors associated with those attitudes have recently been examined among undergraduate students in the profession, but not among clinicians in practice. Aims: To examine whether AI literacy and AI anxiety are independently associated with attitudes towards AI beyond prior AI use, self-directed AI learning and formal AI training, and whether the two are differentially related to the positive and negative dimensions of those attitudes. Methods & Procedures: A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 180 SLTs in Türkiye, recruited by convenience and predominantly early in their careers (mean age 25.4 years), using the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale and the General Attitudes towards Artificial Intelligence Scale (GAAIS). Hierarchical multiple regressions were complemented by comparisons of each construct’s correlations and adjusted coefficients across the two attitude dimensions, sensitivity analyses and post hoc confirmatory factor analyses. Outcomes & Results: Beyond the experiential variables, AI literacy and AI anxiety explained an additional 15.2% of the variance in positive attitudes, with AI literacy the only independent correlate (β = .403, p < .001), and an additional 42.1% of the variance in attitudes towards AI-related drawbacks (reverse-scored, so that higher values indicate fewer concerns), with anxiety the only independent correlate (β = −.679, p < .001). Each construct was significantly more strongly associated with one dimension than with the other, in both zero-order correlations and adjusted coefficients (all p ≤ .001). None of the AI-related experiential variables remained significant. The pattern held across sensitivity analyses, in which one year or more of professional experience was also associated with more positive attitudes. Absolute fit was poor for the GAAIS and AI literacy measurement models and mixed for the AI anxiety model. Conclusions & Implications: In a predominantly early-career, private-sector sample of Turkish SLTs, self-reported AI literacy and AI anxiety were differentially associated with attitudes towards AI, each related primarily to a different attitude dimension. These patterns require cautious interpretation, because the anxiety and negative-attitude measures, although empirically distinguishable, share item content and substantial variance, and because the literacy measure indexes general rather than clinically situated competence. AI literacy and AI-related concerns may still be complementary targets for education supporting clinically responsible integration of AI into SLT.

items.title: AI Predictive Maintenance for Smart Factories
items.abstract: Unexpected equipment stoppages can interrupt production, increase maintenance costs and reduce manufacturing consistency. This paper presents a low-cost Internet of Things (IoT) prototype for machine-condition monitoring as a foundation for predictive maintenance in smart factories. The prototype uses an ESP32 microcontroller connected to a DHT22 temperature-and-humidity sensor, an SW-420 digital vibration detector and an ACS712 current-sensor module. A low-voltage DC motor is driven through an L298N module, while LEDs and a buzzer provide local threshold-based indications. The ESP32 periodically sends a JSON payload over Wi-Fi to a FastAPI service hosted on a Mac computer. The backend exposes endpoints for receiving the latest sensor data and retrieving historical records, which are stored in an SQLite database. A Streamlit dashboard displays the latest measurements and supports historical visualization. During implementation, sensor readings were visible through the serial monitor, the HTTP POST request returned status code 200, and the history endpoint returned stored records. These observations demonstrate the operation of the core data pipeline. The current prototype performs monitoring and rule-based alerts; a trained and validated artificial-intelligence model has not yet been implemented. In addition, the current field from the ACS712 represents a raw analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) reading rather than calibrated amperes. Future work includes sensor calibration, longer-term data collection, fault-labelled experiments, anomaly detection, and validation of machine-learning methods against documented operating conditions.

items.title: AI-Based Intelligent Crop Selection Using Market and Environmental Analysis
items.abstract: Agriculture is essential in economic growth and food availability, particularly in India, where a significant percentage of the population depends on farming for their livelihoods. However, agricultural communities encounter various difficulties, such as climate variability, irregular rainfall, soil degradation, water scarcity, and fluctuating market prices. Traditional crop selection methods often depend on traditional knowledge and traditional farming methods, which may may not sufficiently consider variations in environmental factors and market demands. To overcome these limitations, this study introduces an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based intelligent crop selection system that combines environmental parameters and economic and market indicators to improve farming decisions. The developed framework examines important environmental variables, including soil nutrient content, temperature, humidity, rainfall, and soil pH, together with financial indicators such as market demand for crops, market price, and expected economic returns. ML-based predictive techniques, including Random Forest, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), are developed and assessed for crop prediction and recommendation. The system is designed to determine appropriate crop varieties by considering environmental compatibility and economic potential, providing farmers with recommendations based on analytical data rather than relying solely on conventional crop selection techniques. The experimental evaluation compares the predictive performance of the implemented models and identifies an appropriate model for crop recommendation. By integrating environmental suitability with market analysis, the proposed approach seeks to improve crop selection, optimize agricultural resource use, reduce cultivation risks, and improve farmers' financial returns for farmers. The system can also be extended through Internet of Things (IoT) technologies and cloud computing to enable real-time environmental monitoring and scalable agricultural applications. This approach contributes to precision agriculture by combining machine learning-based prediction with environmental and economic analysis to promote sustainable farming practices and informed agricultural decision-making.

items.title: AI-Based Strategies for Process Optimization in Non-Traditional Machining of Smart Materials
items.abstract: The recent trend that has increased the use of smart materials in sophisticated engineering systems requires machining systems that are highly accurate, scalable, and have high levels of process reliability. The traditional machining methods find difficulties with smart materials such as shape-memory alloys (SMAs), piezoelectric composites, magnetorheological materials, and advanced ceramics because of excessive tool wear, thermal degradation, and low process control. The shaping of these materials can be achieved with greater flexibility in non-traditional machining (NTM) processes, such as electrical discharge machining (EDM), laser beam machining (LBM), ultrasonic machining (USM), and abrasive waterjet machining (AWJM), although robust performance is not yet achieved because of nonlinear interactions within the processes. The recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI) have presented new opportunities for optimizing these processes with the help of data-driven modeling, adaptive control, and real-time decision-making. This chapter reviews AI-based strategies for optimizing NTM processes applied to smart materials and especially emphasizes hybrid and multi-objective optimization models. The techniques of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), fuzzy logic, evolutionary algorithms (EAs), and reinforcement learning (RL) are mentioned in relation to making the choice of process parameters, predicting surface quality, minimizing defects, increasing productivity, and improving energy efficiency.

items.title: AI-Enabled Geospatial Monitoring Framework for On-Board Housekeeping Services in Indian Railways
items.abstract: With the rapid advancement of computer vision and artificial intelligence (AI) systems, a significant research is conducted in this domain, such as monitoring railway tracks, maintenance, and routine inspection. The combination with other technologies, such as deep learning, Internet of Things (IoT), and machine learning, has enhanced passenger comfort, safety, and service quality. In addition, the combination of Geographic Information Systems (GIS) provides spatial mapping, visualization on a real-time basis, and location-based analysis of conditions among train coaches, routes, and boarding stations. This geo-tagging information helps in decision-making by detecting high-demand zones and resource allocations. Among these, housekeeping plays a vital role in railway systems in terms of enduser satisfaction. This chapter presents an AI-based monitoring system for on-board housekeeping services provided by Indian Railways. This chapter presents a GIS- and AI-enabled monitoring framework for standardized and traceable assessment of cleanliness conditions in railway coaches. Images are captured through a mobile application and automatically tagged with timestamp, train number, coach identification, and GPS coordinates. The GPS coordinates are used to establish the authenticity of the images for their location and time of capture inside the train. A deep learning model based on ResNet34 architecture was trained to assess cleanliness conditions of key coach components, namely toilets, washbasins, and dustbins, and classify them into three categories: good, average, and poor. The model was trained using a dataset of 3,920 images collected from operational train environments and annotated by end users. The dataset was divided into 3,108 images for training and 782 images for validation. The experimental evaluation achieved an accuracy of 67.6%. items.title: AI-Generated Deception
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed the technological landscape of the world. Advances in generative technologies allow AI to create text, images, audio, and video that closely resemble human-authored content with the click of a button. These capabilities have revolutionized many fields, offering content at a fraction of the cost and time. Although AI promises countless benefits, its rapid integration into daily life has surpassed society’s capacity to thoroughly examine the potential consequences. This chapter examines how, in the wrong hands, AI creates unprecedented opportunities for deception, posing far-reaching risks to political, environmental, economic, social, and interpersonal ecosystems worldwide. The political consequences are analyzed in a macro context, with special attention paid to AI manipulation, including targeted misinformation, algorithmic polarization, minority representation, and deepfake propaganda that threaten democratic processes and public trust. Environmental consequences of AI are touched on including the burden data centers place on water and electrical resources, impacting surrounding communities and the ecosystem. This chapter further explores the economic consequences of AI deception, highlighting consumer fraud, financial exploitation, decline in institutional trust, and market instability. The social consequences are examined from a variety of perspectives, beginning with the driving factors behind the creation of and engagement with AI-created content including how attention-seeking, social validation, and algorithmic amplification normalize misinformation and reinforce division. Lastly, AI deception is examined in relation to its expanding role in providing intimacy, emotional support, romantic connection, and sexual material to its users, shedding light on its disturbing consequences including non-consensual pornography and harmful mental health advice. The chapter concludes by discussing ethical, legal, and psychological implications of AI deception, emphasizing media literacy, critical awareness, boundary-setting, and accountability as essential strategies for mitigating harm while preserving human agency in an AI-influenced ecosystem.

items.title: Alzheimer's Disease Surveillance Using CDC Data and Hybrid Ensemble Models
items.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a problem that will be very hard to deal with globally in public health, but most AI (Artificial Intelligence) solutions for AD prediction are still based on neuroimaging methods (e.g., MRI and PET) that are very expensive. This restricts the use of AI for monitoring at the population level. Hence, there is a need for predictive frameworks that can rely on public health data, which are available in tabular format, to forecast the trends of diseases like AD affecting the population. In this research, we put forward a Dual-Stream Hybrid Ensemble Framework for the adoption of Alzheimer's disease predictive methods by longitudinal CDC data (2015–2022). The research works on checking the ability of modern deep learning architectures to outperform the strong Gradient Boosting Machine baselines on complex epidemiological tabular datasets. The framework consists of a Feature Tokenizer Transformer (FT-Transformer) joined with three leading GBMs (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) and a deep Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). To maintain the validity of the scientific findings, we impose a strict “Chinese Wall” feature segregation rule to avoid data leakage by disabling the use of context-specific proxy identifiers in the binary classification stream. Furthermore, Probability Target Encoding and Cost-Sensitive Learning methods are put into practice to tackle high-cardinality categorical features and severe class imbalance issues (~1:9.5). The outcomes of the experiments indicate that the FT-Transformer provides the best regression performance with an R-squared value of 0.9451, while XGBoost gives a lower value of 0.8752, and the final weighted regression ensemble provides an R-squared value of 0.9394. For classification under leakage constraints, the cost-sensitive ensemble reaches high sensitivity at the cost of precision at Recall = 89.75%, thereby indicating a demonstrates utility for identifying AD/SCD-related surveillance strata even though metadata proxies have been removed. To sum it up, the new research results give empirical evidence that deep learning by transformers can outperform classic boosting methods for public health monitoring of Alzheimer’s disease if the right tokenization and training restrictions are applied.

items.title: An Application of the Self-Determination Theory Model for AI-Enhanced, Digital Psychosocial Interventions for Pediatric Disabilities
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Youth with developmental disabilities (DDs) experience elevated psychosocial challenges, including difficulties with emotion regulation, self-concept, and access to timely mental health support. Pediatric nurses are well-positioned to address these needs; however, time constraints, limited training, and restricted access to specialty services often impede the provision of consistent psychosocial care. Digitally delivered psychosocial interventions enhanced by artificial intelligence (AI) offer new opportunities for individualized, accessible support, but these approaches frequently lack a clear theoretical foundation. PURPOSE: This paper applied Self-Determination Theory (SDT), specifically Basic Psychological Needs Theory, to guide pediatric nurses' use of AI-enhanced, digital psychosocial interventions for DDs in practice. METHODS: A theory-driven synthesis mapped SDT needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness) to AI-enabled intervention features: conversational agents, neuro/adaptive feedback, and emotion-recognition tailoring. RESULTS: The framework specifies how these features can promote volitional engagement, optimal challenge with timely feedback, and supportive interactions for youth with DDs. It also notes evidence gaps (small, heterogeneous samples; limited comparisons and follow-up) and barriers involving payment/workload, equity and access, and data protection, transparency, and bias. CONCLUSIONS/IMPLICATIONS: SDT offers a coherent, testable foundation for designing, evaluating, and integrating AI-enhanced psychosocial supports for pediatric DDs. Nurses can screen for support, coach families, monitor risks, and advocate for ethical deployment and rigorous research.

items.title: An Ecocentric Assessment Framework for Artificial Intelligence and Computational Design in Architecture
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) supports environmental performance prediction and the evaluation of alternatives in architectural design. However, improvements in energy or carbon indicators alone do not demonstrate that non-human life holds independent value in design decisions. This chapter examines AI and related computational design approaches in architecture from an ecocentric perspective through a focused narrative review and conceptual synthesis supported by a structured database search. The 375 raw records retrieved from Scopus and Web of Science were reduced to 256 unique records; following title and abstract screening, a final purposive selection of 19 studies was established. Together with one supplementary publication, the 20 documents were examined under the themes of performance and decision-making, life cycle boundaries, the representation of non-human life, habitat geometry and materials, time and maintenance, and visual generation and ecological validation. The synthesis informs a preliminary ecocentric assessment framework comprising three dimensions: stakeholder scope, integration of environmental and ecological impacts into decision-making, and ecological responsibility. By distinguishing computational success from ecological outcomes, the framework provides an analytical basis for examining who benefits from design decisions, how environmental and ecological requirements influence those decisions, and how responsibility for their outcomes is addressed.

items.title: An Impactal study on Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) in the Context of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) have substantially influenced artificial intelligence by enabling computational systems to learn representations from images, language, behavioural sequences, and other complex data. This paper presents a selective narrative review of their conceptual development, applications, evaluation requirements, and societal implications. It synthesises foundational and application-oriented publications concerning computer vision, natural language processing, healthcare image classification, financial prediction, cybersecurity, and reinforcement learning. The review uses a qualitative comparative framework to examine the task addressed, the evidence reported, and the conditions limiting interpretation. The reviewed literature illustrates the value of learned representations and task-specific architectures, while also showing why benchmark performance cannot alone establish operational reliability or social benefit. Cross-cutting concerns include data quality, distribution shift, interpretability, subgroup disparities, adversarial vulnerability, privacy, and computational requirements. The paper proposes a practical evaluation framework connecting task suitability, data provenance, appropriate baselines, external validation, human oversight, and monitoring after deployment. No new model training, expert interviews, public-opinion survey, or pooled statistical analysis is reported. The synthesis concludes that the contribution of ANNs should be assessed through performance under relevant operating conditions and the consequences of their use, rather than through accuracy alone. Keywords: artificial neural networks; artificial intelligence; deep learning; representation learning; model evaluation; responsible AI.

items.title: AN LLM-BASED FRAMEWORK FOR AUTOMATED RECOGNITION AND STRUCTURING OF CONSTRUCTION COST ESTIMATES
items.abstract: The construction industry continues to encounter considerable inefficiencies associated with the manual interpretation and processing of heterogeneous cost estimation documentation, which is characterised by a paucity of background data. The present study puts forward a Large Language Model (LLM)-based framework for the automated recognition, semantic structuring, and enrichment of construction cost estimates originating from unstandardised Excel spreadsheets. The proposed framework uses a combination of domain-specific data annotation, machine learning-assisted document understanding and semantic similarity retrieval to convert semi-structured procurement and estimation documents into standardised, machine-readable datasets. A large corpus of historical construction estimates was collected, organised and manually labelled to create a training dataset for the LLM-based recognition pipeline. An API-oriented architecture automatically parses, classifies and converts uploaded spreadsheets into structured entities, including estimate positions, quantities, units, unit costs and total costs. The framework also incorporates a semantic similarity matching mechanism that compares newly uploaded estimates with historical priced estimates stored in the reference database. Consequently, the system can automatically suggest historically relevant unit prices and related CO₂ indicators for similar construction positions. Experimental validation has demonstrated that the proposed framework achieves a semantic position-matching accuracy of over 85%, enabling the automatic completion of 50–70% of newly uploaded estimates. Furthermore, the solution reduces the effort required for manual estimation by around 70% compared to traditional workflows. The findings suggest that using LLM-assisted recognition and historical knowledge retrieval can substantially improve the productivity, consistency and sustainability of construction cost management and procurement processes.

items.title: ANIMAL TRANSLATOR USING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: SMART TECHNOLOGY TO INTERPRET ANIMAL BEHAVIOR AND SOUNDS
items.abstract: Animal communication takes place via vocalizations, body posture, movement, facial expressions, and context. Although there are some animal communications known to humans, decoding the internal state of an animal correctly may be challenging, especially if there are different species of animals. An idea of an AI Animal Translator is introduced in this paper. It is supposed that the system would perform audio analysis, computer vision, machine learning, and other context-related operations to classify the animals' sounds and behaviour into understandable human messages like hunger, fear, pain, stress, comfort, alertness, or any social activity. The proposed system would include data collection, preprocessing, features extraction, multimodal classification, confidence assessment, and alerting for users. This device should be used as an auxiliary system to help people to better comprehend animals' communication, but not as a direct translation from one language to another. The review of related scientific trends, the problem statement, the architecture of the proposed system, evaluation methodology, applications, limitations, ethical considerations, and further research are covered in the paper.

items.title: Application of artificial intelligence in predicting periodontal risks in orthodontic patients: a scoping review
items.abstract: Introduction This scoping review aims to evaluate artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning, for predicting periodontal risks in orthodontic patients and to identify methodological gaps limiting clinical translation. Methods Reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR and PRISMA-S guidelines, a systematic search was conducted across six electronic databases (PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase, Cochrane Library), grey literature, and citation tracking (Jan 1, 2018–June 1, 2025). Out of 880 identified records (312 duplicates removed; 568 screened), 56 full texts were evaluated, yielding 3 core clinical CBCT studies meeting strict eligibility criteria (Xu et al., 2024; Pirayesh et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025). Methodological quality and risk of bias were appraised using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Results Reported performance for orthodontically induced inflammatory root resorption (OIIRR) ranged from 82.1% accuracy in small canine-induced resorption cohorts to >94% accuracy in larger grading frameworks. However, critical appraisal revealed a high risk of bias across all studies due to single-center retrospective designs, lack of independent external validation, and missing calibration metrics. Direct clinical evidence for AI prediction of gingival recession or orthodontic alveolar bone loss was insufficient within strict pre-cutoff parameters. Discussion While AI demonstrates technical feasibility for assessing orthodontically related root resorption risk, robust individual-level risk prediction remains unestablished. Prospective multicenter external validation and adherence to standardized reporting guidelines are required prior to routine clinical adoption.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Integration in Education: Teachers’ Utilization, Perceptions, and Implementation Challenges
items.abstract: This study explored the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in chemistry instruction, focusing on teachers’ utilization patterns, perceptions, and the challenges they encounter. A sample of 18 chemistry teachers from various institutions participated, providing insights into the types and frequency of AI tools used, including ChatGPT, ChemCollective, and PhET Interactive Simulations. Findings indicate that generative AI tools—particularly ChatGPT—are the most widely adopted due to their accessibility, versatility, and ease of integration. In contrast, subject-specific and creative AI platforms remain underutilized, suggesting that familiarity, perceived complexity, and awareness significantly influence adoption patterns. Teachers demonstrated strongly positive perceptions of AI integration in both curriculum and instruction, recognizing its potential to enhance content delivery, student engagement, personalized learning, and the development of 21st-century skills. No significant differences were found across institutions, indicating a shared readiness to integrate AI in chemistry education. Despite these favorable perceptions, effective implementation is constrained by technical limitations, infrastructure gaps, data quality concerns, usability challenges, ethical issues, and privacy risks. Teachers also expressed concerns about over-reliance on AI and the potential reduction of meaningful teacher–student interaction, emphasizing the importance of maintaining a balanced, human-centered approach. Overall, the findings support the strategic and guided adoption of AI as a pedagogical enhancement tool rather than a substitute for professional judgment and instructional expertise. The results highlight the need for structured, discipline-specific professional development that emphasizes prompt literacy, critical evaluation of AI outputs, ethical awareness, and pedagogical alignment. Strengthening technological infrastructure, establishing sustained institutional support systems, and developing clear guidelines for responsible AI use are essential to ensure effective, equitable, and ethically grounded integration of AI in chemistry education.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption and the Financial Performance of Commercial Banks in Kenya
items.abstract: Commercial banks in Kenya have invested heavily in artificial intelligence (AI), yet sector profitability has weakened, with average return on assets (ROA) falling from 3.3 percent in 2021 to 2.6 percent in 2024. This research investigated the effect of AI adoption on the financial performance of commercial banks in Kenya. Specifically, it examined the effects of AI-enabled customer service, machine learning credit scoring, robotic process automation and AI-driven fraud detection on financial performance, measured by ROA, as well as the mediating effect of operational efficiency and the moderating effect of bank size. A census of all 38 commercial banks licensed by the Central Bank of Kenya was undertaken, using data from audited annual reports and Central Bank of Kenya supervisory returns. Data were analysed using random effects panel regression with cluster-robust standard errors, the causal steps approach supplemented by the Sobel test, and moderated regression. AI-enabled customer service had a positive and significant effect on ROA (β = 0.927, p = 0.003). Machine learning credit scoring (β = −0.046, p = 0.841), robotic process automation (β = −0.450, p = 0.098) and AI-driven fraud detection (β = 0.137, p = 0.459) had no significant effects. AI-enabled customer service lowered the cost-to-income ratio (β = −0.194, p < 0.001), but operational efficiency did not significantly mediate its relationship with ROA (Sobel z = 1.287, p = 0.198). The interaction between AI adoption and bank size was not significant (β = 0.154, p = 0.589). The study concluded that the effect of AI adoption on bank performance is application-specific. Only customer-facing AI translated into higher profitability, while the credit scoring, process automation and fraud detection applications did not. Operational efficiency did not mediate, and bank size did not moderate, the connection between AI adoption and performance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation in Smart Tourism Destination Management: An Integrative Review and the AI-SDM Framework
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming tourism destinations through personalized services, conversational and generative interfaces, predictive analytics, and data-driven decision-making. Yet technology adoption alone does not explain how destinations convert AI-generated information into coordinated managerial action. Objective: This study addresses that organizational problem through a conceptual integrative review of research on AI-enabled tourism services, smart destination management, destination governance, visitor experience, organizational capabilities, workforce readiness, and responsible data practices. Methods: The synthesis identifies four interconnected application domains: AI-driven personalization, conversational and generative visitor interaction, predictive visitor-flow analytics, and data-driven destination governance. These domains are abstracted into the AI-Enabled Smart Destination Management (AI-SDM) framework, which connects AI-Enabled Service Capability, Smart Destination Governance Capability, and Visitor Experience Outcomes. Results: Visitor and operational intelligence functions as the principal conversion input, while visitor-generated behavioral and experiential feedback supports subsequent organizational learning and AI adaptation. Workforce AI Readiness and Responsible Data Governance are positioned as enabling conditions. The framework contributes to destination-management theory by shifting attention from AI adoption toward the organizational capability required to sense relevant visitor information, interpret and coordinate responses, and responsibly convert intelligence into destination action and visitor value. It complements broad smart-tourism and emerging cognitive-destination architectures by specifying the organizational intelligence-to-action mechanism that links AI-enabled interactions with destination governance and learning. Conclusion: The paper concludes with propositions and an empirical research agenda for measurement development and validation.

items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Digital Twin (DT) technologies are transforming advanced manufacturing by enabling intelligent, data-driven, and sustainable production systems. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the synergistic integration of AI algorithms with cyber-physical Digital Twin frameworks across key manufacturing domains, including additive manufacturing, microwave hybrid heating, robotic machining, and metal cladding. AI-driven models facilitate real-time defect detection, predictive maintenance, adaptive process control, and parameter optimization, while Digital Twins provide high-fidelity virtual replicas for simulation, synchronization, and closed-loop decision-making. The convergence of these technologies enables predictive and prescriptive manufacturing strategies, reducing waste, improving energy efficiency, and enhancing product quality. Furthermore, the study examines system-level integration architectures, cloud–edge computing infrastructure, and emerging approaches such as physics-informed neural networks and federated learning. The transition toward Industry 5.0 is discussed, emphasizing human-centricity, sustainability, and ethical AI deployment. The findings highlight AI–DT integration as a foundational pillar for intelligent, resilient, and environmentally responsible manufacturing ecosystems.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Green Water-Use Efficiency in China: Provincial Evidence from 2011–2024
items.abstract: Whether artificial intelligence (AI) alleviates or aggravates resource constraints is an open and increasingly consequential question: AI carries a substantial energy and water footprint, yet it may also raise resource-use efficiency through prediction, intelligent optimization, and better allocation. Using a balanced panel of 30 Chinese provinces over 2011–2024, this study measures green water-use efficiency (GWUE) with a Super-SBM model and estimates the association between AI development and GWUE using two-way fixed effects, complemented by an instrumental-variable strategy and interpretable machine learning. We find that AI development is associated with a significant improvement in GWUE: a one-standard-deviation increase in the AI index corresponds to a 3.8% rise in GWUE. The relationship is consistent with two channels—green technological innovation and environmental-governance capacity. The association is stronger where per-capita water use is higher, and differs across regions of differing industrial water dependence and computing infrastructure. XGBoost–SHAP analysis further suggests a nonlinear transition around an AI development level of approximately 0.12, beyond which AI’s marginal contribution to predicted GWUE becomes increasingly positive. These findings indicate that AI does not automatically become a green technology; its resource-efficiency dividend depends on the resource and technological environment in which it is deployed.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and machine learning-enabled smart nanodrug delivery systems for tissue regeneration and precision therapeutic release
items.abstract: Rational nanoparticle design, stimuli-responsive release control, and release kinetics matching with changing tissue microenvironment are improving preclinical and clinical regenerative therapy results and clinical translation utilizing artificial intelligence and machine learning. This review is intended to explore the use of interdisciplinary strategies that integrate computational design and experimental validation to advance tissue-focused drug delivery systems. Using AI-enabled procedures to increase encapsulation efficiencies and tunability of release and target engagement has led to the acceleration of the inverse design and closed-loop optimization processes in numerous preclinical models. Unfortunately, sparse metadata and tiny heterogeneous datasets restrained repeatability. Incompetent benchmark repositories, inconsistent reporting, and data sharing pipelines. The regulatory paths for algorithm-informed device-drug products are new and require models, quantification of uncertainty, sterilization validation, and clinical-grade stability data. The pragmatic roadmap emphasizes short-term metadata standards, intermediate community-based benchmarks, and long-term adaptive clinical trials linking computational outcomes with biomarker-driven goals. A consolidated series of technical, translational, and governance recommendations is presented with an actionable checklist made for bridging computational design with clinical translation, such as a synthesis of governance and experiments checklist, which has never been seen before, for faster real-world implementation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Mental Health: Research Trends, Hotspots, and Emerging Themes (2004–2024)
items.abstract: Background and Aims: Mental health disorders constitute a major global health burden, while mental health services remain inadequately resourced, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), including machine learning, deep learning, and natural language processing, have opened new possibilities for the early detection, diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment of mental health conditions. Despite rapid growth, research in this field is highly interdisciplinary and fragmented, limiting understanding of its overall development. Methods: A retrospective cross-sectional bibliometric analysis was conducted using the Scopus database. Peer-reviewed journal articles published between January 1, 2004, and December 31, 2024, were retrieved through title-based searches combining AI- and mental health-related terms. Bibliometric indicators, including publication output, authors, institutions, countries, journals, funding agencies, and highly cited articles, were analyzed. Science-mapping techniques and network visualization using VOS viewer were employed to explore intellectual, social, and conceptual research structures. Results: A total of 14,904 publications were included. Research growth was modest until 2015 but accelerated markedly after 2019 (R² = 0.9685). The field was dominated by medicine, neuroscience, and computer science. The United States, China, and the United Kingdom emerged as the leading contributors in both productivity and international collaboration. Key research hotspots included AI-driven neuroimaging, natural language processing for mental health assessment, social media–based surveillance, and digital mental health interventions. Conclusion: AI research in mental health has expanded rapidly, progressing from neurobiological modeling to scalable digital applications. Future advancement will require ethical governance, representative datasets, interdisciplinary collaboration, and robust clinical validation to ensure safe, effective, and equitable implementation.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and synthetic biology for integrated crop improvement
items.abstract: Conventional crop breeding has delivered substantial yield and quality gains but faces persistent constraints from long breeding cycles, limited genetic diversity, and increasing climate volatility. Artificial intelligence (AI) and synthetic biology (SynBio) are emerging as complementary technologies that can accelerate allele discovery, trait design, and deployment across major staples and under-researched crops. Machine learning, computer vision, and robotics support high-throughput phenotyping from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery and mobile devices, while genomic prediction models that integrate multi-omics and climate data can improve selection accuracy for traits such as yield stability and stress tolerance. SynBio platforms enable precise genome editing, synthetic circuits, and metabolic pathway engineering, with applications ranging from biofortified rice to multiplex editing in maize and pangenome-informed breeding in orphan crops such as chickpea and pearl millet. Their convergence, often described as “Breeding 5.0,” supports AI-guided design–build–test–learn (DBTL) cycles that optimize ideotypes for resource efficiency, resilience, and nutrition while reducing reliance on agrochemical inputs. This narrative review outlines the evolution from classical to molecular breeding, synthesizes current AI–SynBio pipelines with illustrative case studies, and highlights persistent challenges in data quality, transformation efficiency, biosafety, regulatory harmonization, and equitable access. We conclude with priorities for inclusive innovation to ensure that climate-smart, nutritious crops benefit diverse agroecosystems responsibly.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and the erosion of professional autonomy in clinical practice – a review and analysis
items.abstract: Professional autonomy is a foundational ethical principle in healthcare, underpinning healthcare professionals’ capacity to exercise independent clinical judgement in light of a patient's particular circumstances, preferences and needs. While ethical debate surrounding medical AI has focused extensively on safety, accuracy and bias, its implications for professional autonomy have received comparatively less attention, a notable omission given AI's growing role in shaping clinical decision-making. This article identifies three salient mechanisms through which AI integration may constrain professional autonomy: (1) algorithmic opacity and explainability, (2) automation bias and de-skilling and (3) institutional pressures. Whilst proposed safeguards such as explainable AI, professional training, system design and institutional governance represent important directions, they do not yet adequately protect professional autonomy. This article therefore calls for closer scrutiny of current approaches to AI integration and for governance frameworks that attend not only to the technical properties of AI systems, but to the organisational and institutional conditions in which they are deployed.

items.abstract: This research evaluates the negative impacts of Artificial Intelligence dependency on the cognitive and academic development of students within the Cameroonian higher education landscape. items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Energy-Efficient Green Cloud Data Centres: A Review of Workload Prediction, Intelligent Scheduling and Cooling Optimization
items.abstract: The rapid growth of online services, digital education and large-scale artificial intelligence has increased the electricity demand of cloud data centres, where servers, storage, networks and cooling equipment run around the clock. Rule-based management policies, which react to fixed thresholds, often leave servers underused and cooling plants over-provisioned. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a different approach: models learn from operational data, anticipate demand and choose actions that save energy while protecting service quality. This review examines how AI is applied to four tasks in a green data centre: forecasting workload, allocating and consolidating virtual machines, scheduling tasks with awareness of energy and carbon, and controlling cooling systems. Statistical forecasting, recurrent neural networks, reinforcement learning and data-driven cooling control are explained and compared through representative studies. An AI-based green-cloud framework is then described that combines a learning-based demand predictor, an energy- and carbon-aware scheduler, a cooling optimiser and a renewable-supply monitor in a closed control loop. A simulation-based evaluation plan using energy, response time, utilization and carbon emission as metrics is outlined. Challenges including data quality, model interpretability, safety of autonomous control and the energy cost of the AI models themselves are discussed.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR STRATEGIC DECISION-MAKING: IMPLICATIONS FOR THE TRANSFORMATION OF BUSINESS MANAGEMENT
items.abstract: In today’s rapidly evolving business environment, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a transformative technological capability with profound implications for strategic decision-making and modern business management. The growing ability of AI systems to analyse extensive volumes of structured and unstructured data, detect intricate patterns, produce predictive insights, and automate analytical activities is reshaping the processes through which organisations formulate and implement strategic decisions. Through the review of recent literature and real-world case studies, this paper critically argues that AI is fundamentally reshaping strategic decision-making and presents a reasoned perspective on how this shift is transforming business management practices and competitive strategies in contemporary organisations. This study also explores the challenges and risks of AI-driven strategic decision-making. The study concludes that the greatest value of AI lies in its capacity to augment rather than replace managerial intelligence. Hence, the study recommends that organisations should adopt hybrid decision-making by combining AI-generated insights with human expertise to enhance decision accuracy, critical thinking, and strategic judgement.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Cybersecurity: A Comprehensive Review of AI-Powered Threat Detection, Cyberattack Prevention, and Information Security
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technologies, cloud computing, interconnected networks, and online services has significantly increased the complexity of modern cybersecurity challenges. Organizations increasingly face sophisticated cyber threats, including malware infections, ransomware, phishing campaigns, unauthorized network intrusions, insider threats, and advanced persistent threats (APTs). Traditional cybersecurity mechanisms, which primarily depend on predefined rules, signature-based detection, and manual security monitoring, often struggle to identify previously unknown attacks and respond effectively to rapidly evolving threats. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), natural language processing (NLP), and behavioral analytics, has emerged as a promising approach for strengthening cybersecurity capabilities.This review examines the application of AI-driven technologies in modern cybersecurity, emphasizing intelligent threat detection, cyberattack prevention, and information security. It explores the role of machine learning and deep learning in network intrusion detection, malware classification, phishing identification, anomaly detection, behavioral threat analysis, and automated incident response. Furthermore, the review investigates emerging developments in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), adversarial machine learning, federated learning, and generative AI, highlighting their implications for developing more adaptive and resilient security infrastructures. Recent academic research published in 2024 and 2025 is considered to evaluate technological developments, practical applications, and emerging limitations.The review identifies several important challenges affecting the practical adoption of AI-based cybersecurity systems, including data quality, model interpretability, false-positive detection, privacy concerns, adversarial manipulation, computational requirements, and the limited generalizability of models across different network environments. The analysis suggests that AI should complement, rather than completely replace, conventional security controls and human cybersecurity expertise. A layered cybersecurity architecture integrating AI-based detection, explainable decision support, continuous model monitoring, and human-supervised incident response may provide a more reliable approach to protecting modern digital environments. Finally, the paper identifies research opportunities related to adversarial robust AI, privacy-preserving collaborative learning, trustworthy generative AI, and autonomous cyber defense.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy by supporting lesion detection, characterization, and clinical decision-making.This narrative review summarizes current evidence on AI-assisted GI endoscopy, focusing on clinical applications, diagnostic performance, implementation challenges, and future directions.Machine learning and deep learning underpin computer-aided detection systems that identify suspicious lesions and computer-aided diagnosis systems that support their characterization.In colorectal cancer screening, the reviewed evidence highlights improvements in adenoma detection and the potential of AI to support optical diagnosis of colorectal polyps.In upper GI endoscopy, promising applications include the detection of Barrett's esophagus-associated neoplasia, early gastric cancer, and other premalignant lesions.Integration with image-enhanced endoscopy further supports real-time tissue characterization and risk stratification.Beyond lesion recognition, AI applications extend to procedural planning, quality assessment, and clinical decision support.Across these applications, data quality, external validation, and algorithm transparency remain central considerations when interpreting diagnostic performance and assessing clinical applicability.The review therefore emphasizes that successful implementation requires both technical development and careful evaluation within clinical workflows, alongside appropriate ethical and regulatory oversight.AI has substantial potential to advance precision endoscopy; however, its contribution to improved patient outcomes requires further clinical evaluation.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN HIGHER EDUCATION THROUGH THE FOUNDATIONS OF BASIC RESEARCH, ECOLOGY AND ACADEMIC CONSCIENCE: A REFLECTIVE COMMENTARY
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly discussed through frameworks of adoption, automation, and organisational reinvention. Their application to higher education requires careful consideration of what education is intended to achieve. This reflective commentary examines McKinsey's three horizons of AI transformation through my experiences in ecological research, university teaching, postgraduate supervision, and academic writing. It develops ten connected arguments concerning scientific foundations, independent learning, field experience, curiosity, institutional resilience, academic conscience, respectful leadership, educational relationships, environmental responsibility, and selective adoption. Selected empirical studies and foundational ecological literature support the discussion, while personal judgments are distinguished from established findings. I argue that faster production of academic material alone cannot demonstrate deeper understanding or stronger research competence. AI can help when its use aligns with learning objectives and is supported by verification, fair assessment, and accountable human decisions. Risks include dependence on generated explanations, weakening of observational skills, restriction of exploratory inquiry, unfair judgments about authorship, increased workload, unequal access, and environmental costs. An ecological perspective also encourages attention to relationships, feedback, and institutions' ability to function when technological services fail. I propose that universities assess AI by what students can explain independently, how reliably they engage with evidence, and the quality of educational relationships. The central responsibility is to preserve the conditions that enable people to become capable researchers and conscientious members of society.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in human resource management: A bibliometric analysis and literature mapping (2015–2025)
items.abstract: Type of the article: Research ArticleAbstractThe integration of artificial intelligence (AI) has profoundly transformed human resource management (HRM) from an administrative function into a strategic decision-making process, creating a critical need to balance algorithmic effectiveness with operational challenges. The purpose of this study is to explore the evolving integration of artificial intelligence within human resource management. This paper utilizes a bibliometric analysis using PRISMA reporting flow guidelines, analyzing data retrieved from the Scopus database for the period from 2015 to 2025. The results reveal an exponential expansion of scientific research over the decade. Out of an initial set of 2,949 publications, 622 relevant documents met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed using VOSviewer. Annual publications grew from nine articles in 2015 to 218 articles in 2025. The geographical distribution shows that India leads the field with 116 publications, followed by China (114) and the United States (98). Furthermore, the thematic mapping identifies nine distinct clusters, with AI and human resource management standing out as the primary domains experiencing transformation. The findings confirm that the field has become a consolidated, dynamic discipline, with strategic implications for organizations seeking to align technological efficiency with organizational justice, ethical considerations, and employee well-being.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in pediatric head and neck tumor imaging: a mini review of current applications and future directions
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is creating new opportunities to enhance medical imaging in pediatric oncology through quantitative image analysis and clinical decision support. This mini review examines the emerging role of AI in pediatric head and neck tumor imaging, including applications in lesion detection and characterization, tumor segmentation and volumetric analysis, treatment planning, longitudinal surveillance, prognostication, and precision medicine. Particular attention is given to the challenges of translating these approaches to pediatric populations, where rare and heterogeneous tumors, limited datasets, variable imaging protocols, and insufficient multicenter validation remain important barriers. We also discuss emerging strategies that may facilitate clinical translation, including federated learning, multimodal data integration, explainable AI, and integration with existing radiology workflows. Although pediatric-specific evidence remains limited, continued multicenter collaboration and prospective validation may enable AI-based tools to provide more reproducible quantitative imaging assessment and increasingly personalized clinical decision support. Ultimately, the clinical value of these technologies will depend on their ability to augment radiologist expertise and improve patient care through responsible integration into routine practice.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in radiology education: from AI-supported learning to clinical innovation—a narrative review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing diagnostic radiology, but education and training have not kept pace. This narrative review brings together current evidence on AI-supported learning in radiology education and how such learning can move into clinical innovation. Surveys from different countries point to the same gap: in a 25-country international survey of radiographers, radiologists, and students, only 10.3% had received formal AI training; in one national survey of Turkish residents, 84.5% had received none. The review maps competency frameworks and curriculum models that define AI literacy and support staged integration into residency. It also assesses AI as a teaching tool, including AI-assisted case-based learning, computer-aided diagnosis training, precision-education knowledge recommenders, and virtual, augmented, and extended reality. Controlled and randomized studies show measurable gains: computer-aided diagnosis training raised resident scores above self-study controls (mean score 52 vs. 38 on a 100-point scale), while an AI-based knowledge recommender shortened reporting time by 162 s per case and relative improvement in graded reporting accuracy scores of 14% (95% CI 8.1–19.8%). Large language models are promising but limited: GPT-4 approaches board-style examination performance (80.6%) yet remains poor at image-based reasoning (47.8%). The review closes by considering how education can feed clinical innovation, along with algorithmic and automation bias, ethical governance, and future research needs. AI education should therefore span the full continuum-from undergraduate training to continuing professional development-if radiology is to innovate safely, effectively, and equitably.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Spinal Diagnostics: Advances, Challenges and Future Directions
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in spinal diagnostics, particularly through machine learning and deep learning applied to medical imaging and clinical data. These technologies may improve the detection and classification of spinal disorders, automate image interpretation and support clinical decision-making. This narrative review summarizes current applications of AI in spinal diagnostics, focusing on methods for detecting spinal cord injuries, spinal tumors, degenerative spine diseases and vertebral fractures, as well as predicting treatment outcomes and postoperative complications. It also examines convolutional and recurrent neural networks, automated image segmentation and other machine learning approaches for analyzing spinal images and clinical information. Available evidence suggests that AI models can perform comparably to conventional methods and expert assessments and may exceed them in some settings. However, implementation remains limited by challenges related to dataset quality and diversity, model generalizability and interpretability, data privacy and regulatory and ethical considerations. This review highlights both the clinical potential of AI and the major barriers to its integration into routine spinal diagnostic practice. Further prospective validation, external testing across diverse patient populations and interdisciplinary collaboration will be essential to establish the clinical utility and ensure the safe implementation of AI-based spinal diagnostic tools.
